Consult Summary:
- 67-year-old female with 5 days of dry cough and persistent rhinorrhea, felt intermittently feverish; probable viral respiratory tract infection with diabetes and hypertension.

History:
- Presenting complaint: 5 days of dry cough (coughing every 20–30 minutes) and constant streaming nasal discharge (reported as green).
- Associated symptoms: intermittent sensation of feeling hot and chills; myalgias; brief diarrheal episode around onset that has resolved; reduced throat discomfort relieved by lemon-based cold remedy.
- Pertinent negatives: no sputum production reported; no hemoptysis; no chest pain; no shortness of breath; no current vomiting or diarrhea; no rash; no headache or visual change.
- Past medical history: diabetes mellitus and hypertension.
- Medications: metformin (dose/route/frequency not documented); lisinopril (patient stated “two hundred” when asked dose — dose/route/frequency not documented; conflict noted).
- Allergies: reports intermittent hay fever; no known medication allergies reported.
- Social history / preventive care: lives with partner and dog; works as an office manager; drinks alcohol “the odd cherry”; smoking status not documented. Recent blood test ~3 weeks ago reported as normal. Recent blood pressure checks not recalled by patient.

Examination:
- Vitals: not recorded.
- Examination findings: none documented.

Impression:
- Probable viral upper/lower respiratory tract infection (doctor noted a likely chest infection; most likely viral). Patient’s diabetes increases risk of bacterial infection — monitor for secondary bacterial infection.

Plan:
- Patient advised to obtain and use a thermometer to check temperature.
- Symptomatic/supportive care: continue lemon-based cold remedy (Lemsip); do not take additional paracetamol-containing products concurrently (Lemsip contains paracetamol). Cough syrup may be used at night only if coughing prevents sleep.
- Safety-netting and red flags for recontact/assessment: seek review if temperature persistently above 37.5–38°C or ongoing/high fevers; if cough worsens or purulent sputum develops; if any hemoptysis or new nose bleeding; if new shortness of breath or chest pain.
- Antibiotics: may be considered if symptoms do not settle or if there is persistent fever/worsening clinical picture given diabetes — will reassess if red flags develop.
- Routine care: ensure regular diabetes and blood pressure monitoring and follow-up with GP as advised.

Quality checks (document_quality):
- Missing but clinically expected elements: measured vital signs (temperature, respiratory rate, pulse, BP, oxygen saturation); smoking status; specific medication doses/routes/frequencies for metformin and lisinopril; formal allergy list (drug allergies specifically clarified); blood glucose self-monitoring status (patient reported no home blood sugar checking equipment).
- Internal conflicts from transcript: patient stated lisinopril as current medication but when asked dose said “two hundred” — likely inaccurate; conflict noted regarding lisinopril dose.
- Transcript quality: generally audible and clear with occasional brief inaudible/uncertain segments; clinical information sufficient for a telephone assessment but lacks objective examination and measured vitals.
